01 / What the raw data covers

Temperature is nearly complete; sunshine is patchy before 1961

The raw JMA files hold 2,216,378 station-days (82 stations × 27,029 days, 1952–2025). Almost every gap in temperature is a block before a station began observing, not a hole in an ongoing record. Only 8 of 82 stations have sunshine data before 1961.

JMA quality codes: 8 = normal; 5 = quasi-normal (a few hourly values missing, still usable); 4 = insufficient data (too many hourly values missing, so the daily value is biased); 1 = missing; 0 = not observed. The cleaning keeps 8 and 5, and treats 4 as missing.

02 / Artefacts to know about

Two issues are flagged, not fixed

The temperature values are internally consistent from 1964 onwards. Before that, and at 27 station relocations, the record changes in ways that could bias a model. The data keeps the values as JMA reports them, and adds flags so the modelling choice is explicit.

Extreme days were checked against neighbours and look like real weather (foehn warm spells on the Japan Sea coast, cold nights at inland Kutchan), so no values were removed as outliers. Each JMA homogeneity number restarts in every one-year download, so changes on 1 January are artefacts of how the data was downloaded and are ignored.

For discussion

Start the modelling period in 1964?

Starting in 1964 avoids the definition change and keeps 4,379 of the 5,192 flowering records. For relocations, the feature table has a relocations_before_season counter that can act as a station-segment effect.

03 / Filling the gaps

Neighbouring stations beat interpolation at every gap length

To choose a method, 1,423 blocks of real observations were hidden and then refilled. The neighbour-difference method (nearby stations' values plus the usual difference between the two stations) averaged 0.80 °C error, and stays flat as gaps grow. Linear interpolation averaged 2.12 °C, and is worse even for a single missing day.

How every in-record temperature gap was handled
Handling (all three temperature variables)GapsDays
left missing: gap > 60 days83313
left missing: no neighbour data149
linear interpolation13
neighbour-difference8591261

Method: for a gap at station S, take up to 3 stations within 300 km with complete data over the gap. For each one, estimate the mean S − neighbour difference over the 60 days either side of the gap, add it to the neighbour's values, and weight by how tightly the two stations track each other. Gaps longer than 60 days are left missing (Onahama 1977–79; Miyakejima 2000–01, during the volcanic evacuation). Every imputed value is labelled in the *_temperature_flag columns.

04 / The climate signal

Late winter has warmed by about 0.42 °C per decade

Averaged across stations, February–March mean temperature has risen by about 2.5 °C since 1964. This is the season that drives bloom timing. It matches the earlier full-bloom trend in the sakura findings report.

05 / Weather and bloom timing

A 1 °C warmer March brings flowering about 3.3 days earlier

Across stations, temperature mostly reflects latitude: warm places bloom early (r = -0.90 for March mean). The more useful question for forecasting is within a station: in a warmer-than-usual year, how much earlier does it bloom? Taking each station's own average out, a +1 °C March anomaly means about 3.3 days earlier, and a +1 °C February–March anomaly about 3.8 days earlier. (Somei-yoshino, 1964–2025, n = 4,377.)

Reading this chart

No linear chill effect does not mean no chill effect

Within a station, a mild January still goes with an earlier bloom. Theory says too little winter chill delays dormancy break, which matters most at the warmest stations (southern Kyushu and the islands). That effect is non-linear and regional, so a straight correlation can miss it. Test a chill × region interaction, or a separate southern model, before dropping the chill feature.

Sunshine has a weak signal and is patchy before 1961. Precipitation is close to zero once station means are removed. Both are candidates to drop.

06 / Decisions & data dictionary

What the team needs to decide

  • Modelling period: start in 1964, and use 1961+ if sunshine is kept.
  • Forecast date: if the model predicts on 1 March, use only the *_feb_end and pre-March features. March features are fine for a "nowcast" analysis but leak information for southern stations.
  • Model structure: use station fixed effects or anomaly features. The raw cross-station correlation mostly reflects latitude.
  • Relocations: ignore, add relocations_before_season as a feature, or drop the 12 large-step breaks.
